title: The silence of complaint files
bodyMd:
Historians studying a city's services often begin with complaint files. Such files are unusually vivid: a broken pump, an impassable lane, or a lamp that never burns appears in a resident's own words. It is tempting to treat a district with few complaints as a well-served district. That temptation confuses the production of a record with the occurrence of the event recorded. The vividness of an individual document can make this problem harder to notice. A named resident describing water entering a kitchen feels closer to lived experience than a table of drainage measurements. That closeness is valuable, but it does not make the surviving speaker typical of everyone who experienced the same condition. The archive contains acts of communication as well as traces of material problems. To count one without examining the other is to assume that every resident had an equal route from experience to an official page, which is precisely what needs investigation.

In the fictional port of Merrow, surviving nineteenth-century complaint books initially suggested that the outer wards had fewer sanitation problems than the prosperous center. Yet a later comparison with street surveys reversed that picture. The outer wards had fewer drains and more recurrent flooding. Their residents also faced greater obstacles to making a complaint: the office accepted submissions during working hours, required a written statement, and charged a small filing fee. Silence in those books could therefore signal restricted access to the reporting system rather than satisfaction with the service.

This does not mean complaint files are useless or that every absence should be interpreted as repression. The central wards' numerous reports still reveal what their residents noticed and what officials were asked to repair. The problem arises when a historian compares raw totals across groups whose opportunities to enter the archive differed. A sound comparison needs information about both the conditions being reported and the machinery of reporting.

There is a further complication. After Merrow abolished its filing fee, complaints rose even as street surveys recorded improved drainage. An analyst looking only at the complaint series might infer deteriorating service. An analyst looking only at the surveys might dismiss residents' concerns as unfounded. Both would miss the interaction: improved access allowed previously unrecorded problems to become visible while infrastructure was improving. Administrative records are neither transparent windows nor worthless distortions. They are products of institutions, and their evidential value depends on reconstructing how those institutions made speaking possible.
